Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
I see that Josh has beaten me to the blow-by-blow from the finals
table. Still, I thought I would file my report on this year's
GenCon.

High points for me:

1. The Player's Guide: The new V:tes strategy tome was unveiled at
the con. That was fun to see. It is a good looking book, filled with
lots of goodies and sage advice. Everyone should grab that when it
comes out. Of course, I am not at all biased by the fact that my name
is in the credits.

2. The Swainbank Draft: Three draft tournaments with the format had
been played before I got there on Thurs., and we played another one on
Sun. It was fun to get the reports. Reviews were somewhat mixed, but
generally positive. The format is intended to cost less, be faster to
draft, let player build good (for draft) decks, still feel like V:tes,
and encourage draft play. The last criterion seems to have been met -
given the workout the format got at the con. Hopefully, it can become
an official format for more drafty goodness.

3. The NAC finals! I was great to be able take a second trip the NAC
finals table. It was a bummer to lose yet again, but it was a good
game. Well played by all. More on that later of course.

Other topics before I get the tournaments themselves:

The Venue: The Con was its usual GenConny self -- overstuffed with
gaming goodness. But after this third trip to Indy I'm ready to see
something new, and excited that we'll be doing our own thing in
Atlanta next year.

2-Day Format: I liked this. I liked that we had 3 big tournaments. I
liked the fact that field got smaller as the days progressed. The deck
variety was good, level of play was high, and I liked the fact that 2
two game wins assured you a spot in the finals and the threshold ended
up even a little lower.

Game Length: I am a firm supporter of the 2 1/2 hour finals. Players
are more talkative, deliberative, and cautious in the finals. At least
one player at the table always has an incentive to make the table go to
time. Its lame for tournament finals to end with a time out. And it
doesn't add much time to the tournament day. Finals should have an
extra 1/2 hour - especially at qualifiers and championships.

The Tournaments:

I don't have the memory or patience for a blow-by-blow but here are
some flavor and highlight clips from my tables - from my own myopic
POV.

Crafted with : Anarch Revolt Deck Builder. [Sun Aug 14 15:03:30 2005]

Round 1. I'd been wondering how the deck would stand up to a real
stealth-bleed predator. I found out in this game. And the answer was
OKish. I took some big bleeds, and couldn't move forward much at all
until I was set up enough to shut down my predator's Malks. She got
ousted by Jeff Thompson playing War Ghouls. Which left me stuck between
Scott Gomes' celerity-guns and Jeff's Ghouls.

Things got worse when they decided to gang up and crush me. I
completely failed to come up with reasonable counter-offer and took my
beating. The guns went on to beat the ghouls and Scott got the table.

Round 2. I was between a Tremere Ally deck and David Tatu playing
Lasombra(?) as my predator. My grand-prey brought out Enkidu but she
didn't do much damage with him. I got upstreamed by my prey a lot,
but my combat was stronger and he mostly got torpor, taken hostage, and
tortured for his efforts. I did a lot of complaining but it mostly
worked out in my favor. Eventually, I dropped the Week of Nightmares
and won the table. I think it was a sweep.

Round 3. In round 3 my prey was playing Assamites. He brought out Joe
Hill and Yazid. Joe took some Earth Sword hits from his fairy prey. I
blocked and dropped him when he tried to hunt and dunked Yazid when he
tried a rescue. Very early, my prey had no minions and not a ton of
pool. What should have been an easy oust turned in to an hour-long
ordeal as his vamps got rescued, he found plenty of untap, my killing
bleeds got stopped with Eagle Site blocks from my predator (Mike Ooi
playing with a merged Hell's Fool!). Finally, I played the Week of
Nightmares and got the oust.

By this time, his prey, Matt Flint playing Kiyasid, had picked up a VP
and was closing in a second one. Matt grabbed my Neighborhood Watch
Command with a Far Mastery and used it to dismember me - forcing my
Ravnos to hunt off each other or knocking the empty ones into torpor.
So, I got stuffed for the second time in a day by another Boston player
and Matt got the table.

I ended up with 1GW and 5 or 6 VP. A solid showing but not enough for
the finals.

Round 1. I am very proud of my round 1 game. I managed to squeeze 2VPs
out of a bad, bad, bad situation. My predator was Matt Hirsh playing a
Tzimisce bleed toolbox with bats and crows fight. My prey was playing
Tzimisce with Starvation of Marnea fight. His prey was an Omaya and
Nadima wall that dropped Smiling Jack early.

I smashed into my prey who seemed to fear the wrath of Omaya and
wasn't going forward. We beat on each others with lots of torpor and
blood loss on both sizes. Meanwhile Matt was bleeding me steadily and
Jack was killing us all, but especially bad for my prey and I, who were
already weak. It looked ugly.

I stopped going forward and started thinking about how to survive
another turn. My grand prey realized Matt was going to run through me
and my prey agreed to my helpful suggestion that he let me Theft blood
off of Omaya to keep me afloat and pay some of the Jack cost. Then he
let my prey burn Jack and his prey - none other than Peter Charnley
and his Arika deck - banished Omaya.

That was my opening and I ran for it. I ousted my prey with some speedy
bleeds and then charged into Nadima. Her fortitude wasn't much help
against my Thefts and Blood Fury and down she went -- allowing me swoop
up a second VP. With the intercept threat gone, Peter's deck really
switched on and he vote-blasted Matt and I off the island and won the
table - announcing "No guts no galaxy!" before he threw down the
big bleed that ousted Matt.

I was happy to walk away with a pair of VPs. And, fortunately, I had
seen Peter and his deck in action. I wouldn't underestimate him
again! No sirreee.

Round 2. Four person table - so I can almost remember everyone. My prey
was Josh Duffin playing Lasombra. He prey was David Tatu - who opened
the game with a delightful Tatuism. Upon learning Josh was playing
Lasombra David announced "You can have anyone else. But I need
Gratiano. I will contest him till the end." Then he brought out
Gregor Anderseen and a few others. No Lasombra in sight.

My predator was Chad? (?) who was also playing Temere and !Tremere. And
his were bigger than mine. I plowed into Josh with a bruise-bleed swarm
and even managed to burn Gratiano, whom Josh had defiantly brought out,
with a Walk of Flame and an assist from NSA Trio. Then I ousted him.

With my quick 1 VP and big DOM behind me I decided to play a little
conservatively. 12 pool, two minions untapped, two Deflections and a
Wake in hand. Its all under control. David KRCs me for 2 and then 2
more. 8 pool. Chad Pentex Subversions one of my vamps and throws down
two Govern bleeds, which I deflect, followed by two Conditioning bleeds
that oust me. Ouch. Stinkin' Dominate bleed. Who plays with that
sleaze?

Round 3. My grand predator was Robyn Tatu playing Maris Streck and
despite the fact that she was being hammered by a stealth-bleed deck,
she managed to get her prey (my predator Mark Loughman playing what
looked like Giovanni Power-Bleed) down to one pool. Robyn bled, Hugh
bounced, and I asked Robyn how much it was worth for me to bounce it
back. Robyn offered 5 turns with no pressure. Sold!

I leapt forward with newfound freedom. Unfortunately my prey was Tobin
Lopes and I leapt headfirst into his Fatima wall deck. Tobin seemed to
have a LOT of untap and Fatima shot the crap out of my poor little
Tremere, and still ousted his prey.

I zapped Fatima with a Burst of Sunlight, and Ignatius got burned by
the bloodhunt when he ate her. But, with Fatima gone I was finally able
to bruise and bleed my way through Tobin. About this time, the 5 turns
of freedom ended and Robyn rightfully crushed what was left of my
broken and dispirited band.

So, 0 GW 4 VP for the day. Not super, but I got me a golden ticket to
day 2. Good enough.

Round1. My predator is Darby Keeney with his patented 1st
Tradition-Pay-to-Play deck. It didn't take him long to get a 1st Trad
on the table and have us all grudgingly fork over 2 pool for the
pleasure of taking a turn. Sadly, tragically, a big bleed got bounced
to him right after he brought out a second, big minion. Darby went down
to 2 pool and couldn't afford to take a turn himself. Oh the irony!
He got ousted.

My new predator was Matt Flint playing what appeared to be the same
deck as me. Lucky for me, I got all the cool vampires first, and Matt
was stuck with an uncontrolled region full of vamps already on the
table. He contested Le Dinh Tho and Rudolpho. I sent my Hordes after
his remaining vamps to get him off the table. Fortunately, that
didn't take too long. Once I got my team back I was able to move
forward pretty easily and picked up the table for a GW and 3VP.

Round 2. This was the Table That Got Away. Early on my prey,
grand-prey, and great-grand prey all got rather low in pool- while my
position was pretty solid. If ever there was a table begging to get
swept this was it. And it was begging me. Ben, it was saying, please
sweep me... please...

I awaken from my daydream to find that my prey, playing Ahrimanes, has
talked his grand-prey (Nick Watkins) into sending a War Ghoul rushing
at him so he could cycle, like, 10 combat cards. This gives him a
handful of untap and intercept - more than enough to stop me from
bleeding him out on my turn. And it buys him time to oust his prey
(Todd Holland - Malk Kindred Spirits bleed). Grrrr... Eventually, I
oust him, and I decide this is as good a time as any to see who my
predator is.. hey its Peter Charnley playing the same Arika deck I saw
yesterday.

Fortunately, since I had faced this deck already, I knew exactly what
to do. Le Din Tho swiped Peter's power cards while I ran through the
table. Just kidding! What actually happened was Nick and I got into a
debate about whether we had a deal, and if we did, was anyone breaking
it. Meanwhile Peter PTOed my Mr. Tho, blasted us with a KRC or two, and
announced "No guts no galaxy!" before throwing a monster Arika
bleed at me. This would have been a great time to be holding a
Deflection. Sadly, the cupboard was bare (hadn't seen one all game.
Bummer). Nick could have blocked with Eagle Site but that wasn't part
of the deal we may or may not have had. I got ousted. Peter got Nick
shortly thereafter.

Round 3. My prey is Jay Kristoff playing Nos Breed-and-Bloat. I set Le
Dinh Tho to work getting rid of those Con Boons while Jay made babies.
My other minions set up an ally intercept wall that totally stymied my
!Toreador bleed-and-vote predator, Shane Schneider. I got Jay with a
series of Really Big Bleeds. Mat Morgan was prey number 2 and held out
for an annoyingly long time- blocking and bouncing my bleeds. I got
down to 4 pool and - here I have give myself a pat on the back for my
Oscar-worthy subtle-yet-nuanced performance as The Man With No
Deflections - right before I woke and bounced a big bleed from Shane
to oust Matt. I was able to finish off my new prey (Will Kristoff
playing Ahrimanes) during my turn.

With the table down the Shane and I, it just seemed like a matter of
time before I got him. But it turned into a matter of too much time.
The table timed out before I could finish him off.

2 GW 7 1/2 VP for the day gets me into...

THE 2005 NAC FINALS

The Seating:

I knew Josh and Jared were playing vote. I didn't know what Stefan was
playing. I knew I didn't want to be between the vote decks, and guesses
Stefan was playing something fast and sleazy. I chose to Jared's prey,
Stefan's predator. I think that was the right call.

Peter Charnley has top seed. As he picks his seat he says "Jared and I
have worked together well before. And I think we can again." He chose
his seat between Stefan and Josh and that probably sealed the game
right there.

The Game

Josh has already blogged up a good overview. But here are my notes:

When I found out Stefan was playing Celerity gun I know my survival
would depend on getting Ambrosious out early to block rushes and
getting Le Dinh Tho out to strip away more rushes - which would leave
Stefan at my mercy -- assuming I didn't get vote-jacked by the three
other vote decks at the table.

I was very happy to seem my opening draw with the deadly Mr. Tho in the
crypt and Ambrosious in my hand. Very happy in indeed. I also got my
intercept locations early which I thought would be great against Jared.
In retrospect I don't think I blocked much that he cared about, and the
intercept locations were mostly a waste of pool.

My anti-rush tech worked as planned. Stefan took two rushes against the
Thoboy but only shot up Ambrosious and Jake Washington with his
efforts.

My problem was that I wasn't hitting my bleed. I had a hand full of
Call of the Hungry Dead all game - completely forgetting that you CAN
cycle Call even if you don't need to. Doh! Eventually, I found my bleed
and took my shot at Stefan. I was a little surprised he decided to
transfer out after my kill-shot got DIed. But I'll take it. I don't
know if Jared could have taken me on his turn or if I could have just
ousted Stefan on my next turn.

As soon as Stefan fell, Peter PTOed Le Dinh Tho for the second time
that day. Ouch. That left me with only Gloria and Andrea as bleeders
and nobody to scout for them. I got ripped by a few votes on Peter's
and the Jared's turns, which brought the table around to what would be
my last turn.

(Astute readers may notice that Josh doesn't have a large role in this
narrative. Frankly, he wasn't getting much done over there.)

My last turn was basically a big stupid-fest. My problem was that I was
jammed on Call, Spectral Intervention, Allies, and Masters. I needed to
nail Peter and needed Bleed cards to do it. From this need to cycle
flowed much idiocy. I played a Hunting Ground - which turned out to be
a rather poor investment of 2 pool. I tried to get the Ericiyes
Fragment from Jared with Andrea (it was Josh's idea. Josh made me do
it) - somehow oblivious to the fact that he had TWO untapped minions
and was sure to block me. He did. Then I tried to get Shambling Hordes
with Gloria - which Jared stopped with a 2nd Trad. Wouldn't it have
been smarter to get the Hordes with Andrea who gets and additional
stealth? And can get by a 2nd Trad with basic Call? Yes. Yes, that
would have been smarter.

The good news was that I had found my bleed cards. I probably ate some
KRC splash on Peter's turn and Josh did nothing special with his
turn... and here we shall pause and consider the table state at the
start of Jared's turn...

Jared had 4 pool and 5 minions. I 5 pool, only Ambrosious untapped, and
no wakes. Peter had 6 pool. Josh 5 pool - Carlton Van Wyk and Gideon
untapped.

If I could survive the turn I had the cards in had to take a run at
Peter's pool. Jared calls the Parity Shift. I convince Josh to try to
block with Carlton - offering to throw Aranthebes and WMRH. The air is
thick with tension. The championship hangs in the balance... and....
Jared plays the Forgotten Labyrinth and dashes all hope of us catching
him. At this point, the really smart play would have been throw the
WMRH intercept anyhow, eat the pool loss and go out of Parity Shift
range! Sadly, I was long done with smart plays for the day. I ate the
pool loss, and a bleed, and got ousted. Later, Jared informed me that
his backup plan was to take Josh's pool and toss it to Peter. And he
had a Major Boon in hand ready for my bleed. But I think he was just
trying to make me feel better.

Peter then ousted Josh with a big Arika bleed - "No guts no galaxy!".
I'm out but the ride isn't over. The Charnley-Strait alliance is ended
and Peter moves in for the kill. It looks like he has the cards in hand
to oust Jared. I'm only seconds away from 2nd place! The time runs
out-- denying Peter the Game Win (but not the tournament win) and
putting me in 3rd, behind Jared.

Congrats to Peter and the rest of the finalist for a good game.

The championship was over but not the Con. On Sunday we had a Swainbank
Draft with Sabbat War and KMW - two great draft sets that gave us a
rather strong and interesting decks. Fun stuff. I didn't make the
finals. But thanks to those who played, and a special thanks to Jeff
(The Lasombra) Thompson who provided the cards, prize support, and ran
the event.

All in all, a great Championship event. Next stop Budapest!

-Ben Swainbank

Ben Swainbank wrote:
> Game Length: I am a firm supporter of the 2 1/2 hour finals. Players

So, by your argument, the problem isn't the two-hour time limit, but
rather the actions of the players. While the "gaseous expansion"
phenomenon won't eat up all of the 30 added minutes, I agree with
Fred Scott that it's largely true that the urgency of decision-making
in the finals only starts appearing with 10 minutes left, when
preliminary-round tiebreakers become more important than the game
win.
For that matter, I think the preliminary-round tiebreakers have a
huge
impact on the length of the finals throughout the finals, and not
just
the last 10 minutes. No matter what, there's always one person - the
person with the best tiebreaker - who wants the finals to go to time.

I personally feel that two hours is a reasonable amount of time for
a final round, and I feel that it's up to the players - and not the
clock - to stop screwing around and play the game. You know what's
at stake. You know who has the best tiebreaker. You know how much
time there is to play. If you want to talk yourself to death, that's

on you, not the rules.

- Ben Peal

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Ben wrote:

> I personally feel that two hours is a reasonable amount of time for
> a final round, and I feel that it's up to the players - and not the
> clock - to stop screwing around and play the game. You know what's
> at stake. You know who has the best tiebreaker. You know how much
> time there is to play. If you want to talk yourself to death, that's
> on you, not the rules.

This is all completely true, but it seems likely that adding a half an hour
is a small enough increment that it won't make that much difference in terms
of player fatigue and event time but *might* just be enough time for some
extra stuff to happen.

Sure, it is possible that the extra half hour will result in the exact same
dynamic of "play slowly till the last 10 minutes and then see what happens",
just for an extra half hour, but it is also possible that a few more games
will actually end--assuming that people are playing consistiently but
cautiously, rather than sandbagging for a time out, the extra half hour
could make a significant difference. On the other hand, if everyone is just
sandbagging for a time out, then it just makes the game go longer before it
times out.

But as, again, it isn't that much of a time increase, and I suspect that
everyone really only cares about doing this to, like, Qualifiers and
Contenental Championships (as opposed to local, 10 player 2R+F events where
the length of the event is often very significant as the venue wants to
close and go home, or whatever), that it seems reasonable to, at the very
least, give it a try. Maybe for the upcoming season, have all the Qualifiers
and Contenental Championships have a 2.5 hour final, see what happens, and
if they all just time out anyway, then go back to 2 hour finals.

Yes, someone (likely Josh) pointed out that having 2 hour rounds and a 2.5
hour final might have an effect on deck performance (i.e. some deck might do
well in a 2 hour game but less well in a 2.5 hour game, or whatever), which
isn't a completely insignificant issue, but still, I suspect it is worth
giving it a try for a season and see what happens.

Indeed. The players (with their decks) demonstrated that they know how
to get GWs within 2 hours in order to get to the finals. Still finals
time out with some frequency.

The NAC timed out in 2001, 2003, 2004, and 2005. The Northeast
Qualifier finals timed out in 2004 and 2005.

I'm sure there are other examples. But these are the ones I'm most
familar with.

I don't its the players and I don't think its their decks. I think its
the finals.

> In my experience at final tables, either people
> play the game and it ends under two hours or people talk the game to death
> and then whoever can sneak in a quick VP wins.

That is not my experience. In the NEQ this year I don't think we talked
that table to death. I think we played conservatively - because we were
smart and none of us wanted to get ousted. Despite having 3 vote decks
on the table I don't think the 2005 NAC table talked itself to death.

A a prelim table everyone is missing a shot at a GW (and other tables
are not) by talking it death or playing slowly. At a finals table,
nobody wants to get ousted, nobody wants to screw up, the guy in the
lead wants to see it go to time with the smallest number of elapsed
turns, and there's more incetive to maintain the balance than let the
table fall.

This results in slower play, even if players aren't overnegotiating or
trying to stall (which they might be).

With a 2 1/2 final it would be harder to time-out the table or play
wait-and-lunge. More turns would mean more games would finish - which
is a more satisfying ending.

The NAC time-out wasn't such a big deal because Peter was already in
the lead. If Jared had been a higher seed it would have seemed most
unfair.

I advocate 2 1/2 hours for all finals, but especially Qualifiers and
Championships. In cost/benefit terms:

Benefits: More finals that result in clear GWs and fewer timeouts (How
many more? I don't know. Lets find out!)

Cost: For players in the finals, getting to play an addition 1/2 hour
(if required) is not a high cost. I, and expect most other players,
would prefer to let the game play out some more.

Players not in the finals don't have to stick around. No cost there.

The Judge is the only one who has to bear any "cost". I would think a
potential extra 1/2 hour tacked onto a long tournament day would not be
too painful. But people who actually run events could say better than
I.

-Ben Swainbank

Simply put, the one difference in the finals is that there is always
someone who wants the round to time out - the person with the best
tiebreaker. As such, there's an inherent amount of "gaseous
expansion"
with respect to using up the allotted time.

The rate of play doesn't accelerate until there are about 10-15
minutes
left, when people realize that they can't play conservatively and
carefully anymore. If we added another half an hour, I'm certain
that
most games that wouldn't have already resolved themselves in two
hours

players decide for themselves to quicken their rate of play much
sooner.
(gee, maybe this is good strategy...)

I also think that people's perception factors in here. Do we
remember
the games that timed out where there wasn't much hope of resolution,
or
do we remember the games where we would have gotten that game win
"...if only I had one more turn"?

As a personal feeling about it all, while it may be more "satisfying"
if a championship finals is played out to a GW conclusion, I haven't
at
all felt that there has been any injustice done by their timing out.
They were all resolved fairly. Everyone knew what was at stake and
knew what the score was when then they sat down at the table. If
they
couldn't demonstrate that they were better than everyone else in the
span of two whole hours (and could someone please tell me how two
hours
is an unreasonable amount of time for a game?), then they didn't
deserve
to win. It's my feeling that players need to be much more mindful of

the clock, much more mindful of the amount of time their turns take,
and much quicker in their rate of play _for_their_own_sake_.

- Ben Peal

In message <2005082909...@fnord.io.com>, Matthew T. Morgan

<far...@io.com> writes:
>It's a criticism I hear and give sometimes. "Nice deck, but I don't
>see how it could take a table in two hours."
>
>It usually means "thanks for making me sit here getting nothing done
>for three hours with your stupid-ass, slow-ass intercept deck!"

IME, technically, there is a vast range of possible deck styles,
covering any length of play speed or whatever.

IME, practically, there are *mostly* decks that sit on their hands and
don't have much forward motion potential at all AND decks that have
forward motion potential but can be played more slowly.

There's also a minor third category of deck - those which explode, with
no longevity. However, these are relatively minor as most players will
easily take a few hints like "Include a handful of blood-dolls and some
Taste of Vitae, okay?"

But that hints at what the problem is with the other two deck types.

Taking the sit on their hands decks specifically. This isn't always
just sitting on their hands. But players have come up with some
ingenious new strategy that involves doing all sorts of cool stuff - but
not ousting their prey. Quite a few players are horror-struck when you
say "Why not cut down some of that cute tech, and shove in some bleed?"
"Butbutbutbutbutbut the whole point of my deck is to make Camarilla
Assamites with guns! YOU'RE MISSING THE POINT!" So, this isn't just
limited to intercept - it's any deck style that doesn't move forward
hard enough, or where the player is more interested in setting up
something cool than setting up something that will win.

So, the hint from Blood Doll relative to the other deck type - the one
that can win OR sit on its hands. Thing is, the most popular pool gain
card in the game is a permanent. Shove in 4-6 Blood Dolls in a deck and
at a few turns in you have 1, maybe 2? Now, you could be a stealth-
bleed player going forward to annihilate the enemy. Yep. Or... when
things get tight, you sit on your hands. Permanent pool gain, hunt with
a vampire each turn (maybe less, with Hungry Coyote, Inbase Discotek, or
whatever other tech you might have), wait. 2 pool back now. Maybe 3
pool back when you cycle down to your third Blood Doll? Wait. Sit.

It's not *just* Blood Doll, of course. There are other options. For
instance, Nikolaus Vermulen and Menele demonstrate other interesting
permanent sit-on-your-hands options.

But Blood Doll is so common amongst decks that any strong deck can ease
back and rely on Blood Doll for some bloat, just waiting and waiting
until a better time comes. But most of the decks in this strong
category can push forward when they need and / or want to. It's just
that cautious play (for whatever reason) can also work out well for
them.

--
